children.translated_text: The Upaniṣadic statement, 'That <s>Brahman</s> is one only, without a second,' surely denies the existence of anything other than <s>Brahman</s>.
Does it not indeed prohibit the real being of something other than <s>Brahman</s>?
Here we reply: when 'without a second' is stated, what compound is intended?

children.text: kiṃ svit tatpuruṣaḥ kiṃvā bahuvrīhir athocyatām ||
children.translated_text: Is it a tatpuruṣa, or is it a bahuvrīhi? Let this be stated.
In the former case, the latter member is first intended as principal.

children.text: padārthas tatra tad brahma tato'nyat sadṛśaṃ tu vā ||
children.translated_text: There the meaning of the word is that <s>Brahman</s>; and what is other than that is either similar to it,

children.text: tadviruddham atho vā syāt triṣv apy anyan na bādhate
children.translated_text: or opposed to it. In all three cases, something other is not negated.

children.text: anyatve sadṛśatve vā dvitīyaṃ sidhyati dhruvam ||
children.translated_text: For in otherness or similarity, a second is certainly established.

children.text: viruddhatve dvitīyena tṛtīyaṃ prathamaṃ tu vā
children.translated_text: If there is opposition, then by means of a second either a third or the first

children.text: brahma prāpnoti yasmāt tad dvitīyena virudhyate ||
children.translated_text: comes to be <s>Brahman</s>, since it is opposed by that second.
Therefore all masses of meanings beginning with a third, together with the first,

children.text: dvitīyena tathā spṛṣṭvā svasthās tiṣṭhanty abādhitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: having been touched in that way by the second, remain in their own place, unnegated.
But, one may object, the negative particle negates absolutely everything other than <s>Brahman</s>,
since the mention of 'second' is an indicator for everything whatsoever.

children.text: naivaṃ niṣedho na hy asmād dvitīyasyāvagamyate
children.translated_text: Not so. For from this no negation of a second is understood.

children.text: tato 'nyat tadviruddhaṃ vā sadṛśaṃ vātra vakti saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Rather, he speaks here of what is other than it, or opposed to it, or similar to it.

children.text: dvitīyaṃ yasya naivāsti tad brahmeti vivakṣite
children.translated_text: If the intended meaning were, 'that <s>Brahman</s> of which there is no second at all,'
then the statements giving characteristics such as truth and the like would fail to be characteristics.
When 'without a second' has as its scope merely the non-existence of what is meant by 'second',
because the meaning of the negative particle rests in itself, there would be no connection with the word <s>Brahman</s>.
There, absence of a second is not a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text: viśeṣaṇe vā tad brahma tṛtīyaṃ prathamaṃ tu vā ||
children.translated_text: And if it were a qualifier, that <s>Brahman</s> would be either a third or a first.
As before, everything would be entailed when the compound is taken as a bahuvrīhi.

children.text: brahmaṇaḥ prathamā ye ca tṛtīyādyā jagattraye ||
children.translated_text: Those who are first in relation to <s>Brahman</s>, and the third and the rest in the three worlds,

children.text: brahma praty advitīyatvāt svasthās tiṣṭhanty abādhitāḥ
children.translated_text: because they are without secondness in relation to <s>Brahman</s>, remain in their own place, unnegated.

children.text: kiṃca tatra bahuvrīhau samāse saṃśrite sati ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, when the bahuvrīhi compound is adopted there,
the meaning of the negative particle, as the meaning of the compound, has no connection with another word-meaning.
When there is a relation with another meaning, the genitive in 'of which' is appropriate.
The non-existence of a second entity is neither <s>Brahman</s> nor a qualifier.

children.text: asattvān na hy asad brahma bhaven nāpi viśeṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: For, because it is unreal, what is unreal cannot be <s>Brahman</s>, nor can it be a qualifier.
Therefore the real existence of the manifold world is not invalidated by the scriptural text of non-duality.
It is established by the force of its own means of knowledge, and is also approved by scripture.
Thus this is said to be the meaning of the scriptural sentence, '<s>Brahman</s> is without a second':
there was not, is not, and will not be anything fit to be counted as a second.

children.text: samo vābhyadhiko vāsya yo dvitīyas tu gaṇyate
children.translated_text: For what is counted as a second would be equal to it or superior to it,
whereas this world is only a minute portion of the manifestation and ordered expansion of its majesty.
How then could it attain the status of being denoted by the word 'second'?
Just as when one says, 'The <s>Cola</s> king is today an emperor without a second on earth,'
the statement is directed to excluding a king equal to him,
not to denying his servants, sons, wives, and the like.
So too the crores of gods, demons, humans, <s>Brahmās</s>, and cosmic eggs,
of the Lord of all, untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruits, and the like,
of <s>Viṣṇu</s>, the storehouse of the six qualities beginning with knowledge, whose manifestation is inconceivable,
are droplets and sprays from the ocean of the greatness of his vibhūti (manifest glory).
Who indeed, counting the seven oceans by bending his fingers,
would count the drops, foam, bubbles, and sprays of their waves?

children.text: yathaika eva savitā na dvitīyo nabhaḥsthale
children.translated_text: Just as, 'The sun is one alone; there is no second in the sky,'

children.text: ityuktyā na hi sāvitrā niṣidhyante 'tra raśmayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: by this statement the sun's rays are certainly not denied here.
Just as, in the counting of what is principally countable, number itself is not counted,
though it exists separately there, like an object other than what is being counted,
so too:
'All beings are one quarter of him; three quarters of him are immortal in heaven.'

children.text: iti bruvan jagat sarvam itthambhāve nyaveśayat ||
children.translated_text: By saying this, scripture placed the whole world in such a state of dependence on him.
Similarly:

children.text: etāvān asya mahimā tato jyāyastaro hi saḥ
children.translated_text: 'So great is his greatness; yet he is greater than that.'

children.text: yatrānyan na vijānāti sa bhūmodaram antaram
children.translated_text: 'Where one does not know anything else, that is fullness'; 'the inner one makes fear for this one manifest,'
and other higher Upaniṣadic texts of this kind,

children.text: meror ivāṇur yasyedaṃ brahmāṇḍam akhilaṃ jagat
children.translated_text: as well as statements such as, 'This whole universe, the cosmic egg, is like an atom in relation to <s>Meru</s> for him,'
all aim to show that everything has such a dependent status in relation to him.
But the world, moving and unmoving, is a mere verbal beginning;
the collection of modifications has as its fixed, underlying reality the root cause alone.
The effect is not other than the cause, like sparks from fire,
as is elaborated through many examples such as clay, iron, seed, and the like.

children.text: nāśakad dagdhum analas tṛṇaṃ majjayituṃ jalam
children.translated_text: Fire was unable to burn a blade of grass, water to sink it,
nor was wind able to move it, without being strengthened by his power.
From knowing one principal thing, everything becomes known:
by such Vedic statements and by trustworthy traditions grounded in them as well,
this manifold world, made of sentient and insentient reality, obtains its being through <s>Brahman</s> as its self.

children.text: iti pramīyate brāhmī vibhūtir na niṣidhyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus it is known to be the divine vibhūti (manifest glory); it is not denied.
If it were denied, then because everything would be false, the transactions of ordinary life and the Veda

children.text: vyavahārās tu lupyeraṃstathā syād brahmadhīr api ||
children.translated_text: would be lost; and so too would cognition of <s>Brahman</s> itself.
The view that because it has practical reality there is no contradiction even if it is false

children.text: pratyakṣāder iti mataṃ prāg eva samadūduṣam ||
children.translated_text: with perception and the other means of knowledge was already thoroughly refuted earlier.
Therefore, by the cognition of <s>Brahman</s>'s non-duality born from the Upaniṣads, the world
is not invalidated, since it is the vibhūti (manifest glory) of <s>Brahman</s>; this is established.

children.text: nanu sattve prapañcasya nāstīti pratyayaḥ katham
children.translated_text: But, if the manifold world exists, how can there be the cognition 'it does not exist'?

children.text: asattve vā kathaṃ tasminn astīti pratyayo bhavet ||
children.translated_text: Or, if it does not exist, how can there be the cognition 'it exists' with regard to it?
The being both existent and nonexistent of one and the same thing is impossible, because the two are contradictory.
For there would be the conjunction of a contradictory pair reached by the cognitions 'existent' and 'nonexistent.'
Because there is no ground for a definite ascertainment of either one of those two meanings,
the <s>Jainas</s> have maintained that the manifest world is both existent and nonexistent.
Putting foremost the apprehension of existence, since the cognition 'it does not exist' also arises,

children.text: sadā sattvaṃ prapañcasya sāṅkhyās tu pratipedire ||
children.translated_text: the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> have maintained that the manifest world is always existent.
In the difficulty caused by the contradictory pair reached by the cognitions 'existent' and 'nonexistent,'
in order to remove the contradiction, by breaking it into aspects of existence and nonexistence,
some have said that the manifest world is indescribable as either existent or nonexistent.
Others, thinking that existence and nonexistence belong separately to a pot and the like

children.text: ghaṭāder iti manvānā vyavasthām apare jaguḥ ||
children.translated_text: through differences of place, time, and so on, have stated a settled arrangement.
Thus, when doubt has arisen from the collision of disputants,
a determination is now made there according to the doctrine of the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>.
If nonexistence and existence were understood in the very nature of a pot,

children.text: syād eva yugapatsattvam asattvaṃ ca ghaṭādiṣu ||
children.translated_text: then existence and nonexistence would indeed occur simultaneously in pots and the like.
But since cognitions such as 'this exists here now' and 'it does not exist' arise
through differences of place, time, and condition, our thoughts are not simply 'it exists' and 'it does not exist.'
Therefore, through difference of place and the like, existence and nonexistence in pots and the like
are fixed in an orderly way; since the objection has been dismissed, there is no impossibility here.
Objection: A relation with place and the like is possible only for what already exists.
It is not accepted that what is nonexistent gains existence because of relation with place and time.

children.text: sambandho dvyāśrayas tasmāt sataḥ sattvaṃ sadā bhavet
children.translated_text: Relation has two substrata; therefore, what exists would always have existence.
That the nonexistent should gain existence from causal factors by birth is exceedingly difficult to maintain.
Therefore the manifest world, having a beginning and an end, is to be placed within the class of the existent.
And it has been said:

children.text: ādāv ante ca yan nāsti nāsti madhye 'pi tat tathā
children.translated_text: What does not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the middle.
Therefore, since its being is ascertained, let it be accepted as always existent.
Thus.
The nonexistence of the nonexistent is eternal, because it is capable of being produced, like a sky-flower.
If it is nonexistent, there is no difference here between prior nonexistence and absolute nonexistence.

children.text: śvetaketum upādāya tat tvam ity api yacchrutam
children.translated_text: And as for what is heard in the sixth chapter, taking <s>Śvetaketu</s> as the addressee, namely 'That thou art,'
how can its primary meaning be possible?
The conscious being denoted by the word 'thou' is afflicted by misery, grief, and pain;
the meaning of the word 'that' is omniscient, whose will is true, an ocean of boundless bliss.

children.text: tatpadārthas tayor aikyaṃ tejas timiravat katham ||
children.translated_text: How can there be identity of those two, like light and darkness?
Whether the differentiating quality is located in the meaning of 'thou,' located externally, or located in the meaning of 'that,'
the single meaning of the scriptural words 'that' and 'thou' is far excluded.
If ignorance, omniscience, suffering, happiness, and the like
are qualifiers of the root-consciousness, or else are mere indicators,
then, because contradictory qualities are transmitted, there would be difference between the meanings of 'thou' and 'that.'
The claim that, by abandoning one part of the expressed meaning, the words 'that' and 'thou' rest in one individual consciousness,

children.text: so 'yaṃ gaur itivat tattvaṃpadayor ity apeśalam ||
children.translated_text: as in the expression 'this is that cow,' is not elegant.
Because contradictory pairs can attach to one and the same qualified subject
through differences of place, time, and condition, the expression 'this is that cow' is appropriate.
But when contradictory pairs are joined to the self-luminous root-consciousness,
there is no determining factor such as place, time, condition, or the like.
If the conscious self is self-luminous and has shaken off every dual pair,
then, since there is no delusion of the evil of duality, scripture would have no object.
By this is also refuted the view that true desire, being the cause of the world, and similar qualities
are superimposed on the supreme when conditioned by <s>māyā</s>, while grief, delusion, and the like, again,

children.text: avidyopādhike jīve vināśe neti yan matam
children.translated_text: belong to the individual soul conditioned by ignorance and vanish; this opinion

children.text: kṣudrabrahmavidām etan mataṃ prāg eva dūṣitam ||
children.translated_text: of petty knowers of <s>Brahman</s> has already been criticized before.
If limiting adjuncts such as <s>māyā</s> and ignorance are imposed on consciousness in its own nature or on consciousness as qualified,
in the former case there is complete confusion, because there is no division between the supreme and the individual soul.

children.text: uttarasminn api tathā viśiṣṭam api cid yadi
children.translated_text: In the latter case also it is the same, if even qualified consciousness
is thought to be consciousness in its own nature, which is without difference, yet as if divided by limiting adjuncts such as <s>māyā</s> and ignorance,

children.text: vibhinnam iva vibhrāntaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ ca iti manyate ||
children.translated_text: deluded, and also qualified.

children.text: taṭasthāvasthitā dharmāḥ svarūpaṃ na spṛśanti kim
children.translated_text: Do qualities standing externally not touch the essential nature?

children.text: na hi daṇḍiśiraśchedād devadatto na hiṃsitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For <s>Devadatta</s> is not uninjured when the head of the staff-bearer is cut off.
The claim that by excluding the unconscious element, consciousness alone remains,

children.text: atas tat tvam asītyāder arthe ity apy asundaram ||
children.translated_text: and that this is the meaning of 'tat tvam asi' and similar texts, is also unsound.
When non-Brahmanhood and non-selfhood are absent, inner consciousness remains.
The pair of words 'that' and 'thou' has as its object the identity of the individual soul and the supreme.
That identity, even in the primary function of those words, rests on two real things.
But the alternative of difference and nondifference that you have raised
is pointless, since bondage is unreal for one who is not different from nondifference.
Nondifference destroys difference in the two things that have become its own substrata;
difference is the mutual non-selfhood of entities. Such is the nature of these two.
Only by first accepting the own nature of the two alternatives, difference and nondifference,
can one refute them; therefore, because your speech is contradicted, you are defeated by contradiction.
Speculation about being different and nondifferent, relation, existence, and nonexistence,
dismissed by direct experience, is mere drying of the throat.

children.text: nīle nīlamatir yādṛgutpale nīladhīr hi sā
children.translated_text: Just as the cognition of blue in a blue thing is indeed the cognition of blue in a lotus,

children.text: nīlam utpalam evedam iti sākṣāccakāsti naḥ ||
children.translated_text: so 'this is a blue lotus' shines forth directly to us.
Although relation by conjunction is known in an object within the range of the senses,
there is the delusion of imposing difficult logical alternatives such as difference and nondifference.
In the same way, when the relation is identity and is rooted in scripture and perception,
the delusion of faulty logical alternatives is warded off by the rod of scripture.
And faultless, unauthored scripture, with the greatest respect,
Again he states what is not true: the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and the individual self.
The liberated self, standing within the pool of <s>Brahman</s>'s bliss, prospers in happiness.
And if, in the result, there is no possessor of the result, liberation would not be a human goal.

children.text: ekaśeṣe hi ciddhātoḥ kasya mokṣaḥ phalaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: For when only the element of consciousness remains, for whom could liberation be a result?

children.text: kiṃca prapañcarūpeṇa kā nu saṃvid vivartate
children.translated_text: Moreover, what consciousness is transformed by appearance into the form of the manifest world?

children.text: na tāvad ghaṭadhīs tasyām asatyām api darśanāt ||
children.translated_text: It is not, to begin with, cognition of a pot, since the world is seen even when that cognition is absent.

children.text: na hi tasyām ajātāyāṃ naṣṭāyāṃ vākhilaṃ jagat
children.translated_text: For when that cognition has not arisen, or when it has ceased,
one cannot say that the whole world does not exist; if one said so, direct perception would refute it.
Nor is it another consciousness, since even when that one is destroyed, others apprehend things.

children.text: nanu saṃvidabhinnaikā na tasyām asti bhedadhīḥ
children.translated_text: Objection: consciousness is one and not different; in it there is no cognition of difference.

children.text: ghaṭādayo hi bhidyante na tu sā cit prakāśanāt ||
children.translated_text: Pots and the like are indeed differentiated, but consciousness is not, because it illuminates.
If cognition of a pot does not appear at the time of awareness of a cloth,

children.text: naivaṃ ghaṭo hi nābhāti sā sphuraty eva tu sphuṭam ||
children.translated_text: it is not so; the pot indeed does not appear, but that consciousness itself shines clearly.
If you say that consciousness excluded from the pot does not shine,
then by the word 'exclusion from that,' is that same consciousness meant, or something else?

children.text: saiva ced bhāsate 'nyaccen na brūhas tasya bhāsanam ||
children.translated_text: If it is that same consciousness, it appears; if it is something else, you do not state that it appears.

children.text: kiṃcāsyāḥ svaprakāśāyā nīrūpāyā na hi svataḥ
children.translated_text: Moreover, for this self-luminous and formless consciousness, there is not, from itself,
apart from the manifoldness of objects, the illusion of apprehending manifoldness.

children.text: na vastu vastudharmo vā na pratyakṣo na laukikaḥ
children.translated_text: Nor is the difference among knowable things such as pots a real thing, a property of a thing, perceptual, or ordinary;
it is only of the nature of error.
Whenever that is so, the arising of apprehension of difference among cognitions depends on that.
How, and still more how, could it have any connection with ultimate reality?

children.text: kiñca svayamprakāśasya svato vā parato 'pi vā
children.translated_text: Moreover, for what is self-luminous, either from itself or from another,

children.text: prāgabhāvādisiddhiḥ syāt svatas tāvan na yujyate ||
children.translated_text: there would have to be establishment of prior absence and so on; from itself, at least, that is not reasonable.
When it exists in itself, absence cannot be established, because the two are contradictory.
And if the self, whose illumination has itself as cause, were absent, that illumination too would be impossible.
Nor can it be from another, because consciousness has no other object-sphere.
Moreover, difference and the like, which belong to what is knowable, cannot possibly be properties of consciousness,
just as color and the like are not; therefore consciousness is non-dual and self-luminous.
Therefore, what has been babbled about difference from it and the like, taking difference in it as a basis,
the knowers of <s>Brahman</s> understand to be this display of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
Ah, this instruction about <s>Brahman</s> is attractive among those who have faith.

children.text: vayam aśraddadhānāḥ so ye yuktiṃ prārthayāmahe ||
children.translated_text: But we are without such faith, we who ask for reasoning.
For each knowing subject and object, cognitions are mutually distinct
and shine immediately, like pleasure, pain, and the like.
In our view, the difference of conjunction, desire, and the like, whose difference is manifested by correlates,

children.text: na hi bhedaḥ svato nāsti nāpratyakṣaś ca saṃmataḥ ||
children.translated_text: is neither nonexistent in itself nor accepted as imperceptible.
If consciousness alone is accepted as all-pervasive and eternal,

children.text: tataḥ sarvaṃ sadā bhāyāt na vā kiṃcit kadācana ||
children.translated_text: then everything would always appear, or nothing would ever appear.
For then a distinction based on the presence or absence of the knowable object
would not fit for cognition, since its greatness would rest on all-pervasiveness like space.
Nor could there be a distinction through a difference of causes, because such causes are absent for what is eternal.
Nor could it be through manifoldness of its own nature, since its oneness has been accepted.
And consequently the deaf and blind would apprehend sounds and other objects,
and distinctions such as teacher and pupil would follow without any cause.

children.text: nanu naḥ saṃvido bhinnaṃ sarvaṃ nāma na kiṃcana
children.translated_text: Objection: in our view there is nothing at all different from consciousness.
Therefore the charge that everything would always appear is made out of place.

children.text: idam ākhyāhi bho kiṃ nu nīlādir na prakāśate
children.translated_text: Tell me this, sir: does blue and the like not appear?

children.text: prakāśamāno nīlādiḥ saṃvido vā na bhidyate ||
children.translated_text: Or, when blue and the like appear, are they not different from consciousness?
On the first alternative, the whole mass of worldly and Vedic usage, pleasant because grounded in cognition,
would not appear at all, since word, meaning, and so forth would not appear.
On the second, the non-duality of consciousness that you desire would be contradicted.
If this manifoldly formed manifest world has consciousness as its self,

children.text: sāpi saṃvit tad ātmeti yato nānā prasajyate ||
children.translated_text: then that consciousness too has that as its self, and therefore plurality would follow.
Nor, because it is a display of <s>avidyā</s>, is it incapable of being defined as different or non-different.
For that <s>avidyā</s>, when touched by the fire of reasoning, becomes like an ornament made of lac.
For example, if this <s>avidyā</s> is held to consist in the absence of knowledge,
then, since its nature is indescribable, it determines nothing at all.
If <s>avidyā</s> is a distinct entity, then it is quite proper to define it as different.
The alternative that it is an entity, a non-entity, and so on is not suitable for it,
while the statement that it is something other than knowledge is very well expressed.
But if even its being a distinct entity is imagined by you through error,

children.text: hantaivaṃ saty avidyaiva vidyā syāt paramārthataḥ ||
children.translated_text: then, alas, in that case <s>avidyā</s> would in truth be knowledge itself.

children.text: kiñca śuddhājaḍā saṃvit avidyeyaṃ tu nesṛśī
children.translated_text: Moreover, pure, non-inert consciousness is one thing, while this <s>avidyā</s> is not such.

children.text: tat kena hetunā seyam anyaiva na nirūpyate ||
children.translated_text: For what reason, then, is this not defined as altogether other?
Furthermore, this <s>avidyā</s> of yours, which has the form of absence and the like,

children.text: sā vidyā kiṃ nu saṃvittir vedyaṃ vā veditātha vā ||
children.translated_text: is that knowledge consciousness, or the known object, or the knower?

children.text: vedyatve veditṛtve ca nāsyās tābhyāṃ nivartanam
children.translated_text: If it is the known object or the knower, it is not removed by those two.

children.text: na hi jñānād ṛte 'jñānam anyatas te nivartate
children.translated_text: For, according to you, ignorance is not removed by anything other than knowledge.

children.text: saṃvid eveti cet tasyā nanu bhavād asambhavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If you say it is consciousness itself, then surely, because that exists, it is impossible.

children.text: kiñceyaṃ tadviruddhā vā na tasyāḥ kvāpi sambhavaḥ
children.translated_text: Moreover, if this is opposed to that consciousness, it can have no existence anywhere,
because the whole world is pervaded by non-dual knowledge alone.
If an absence or something else opposed to consciousness is accepted,
then cast far away the thesis of the non-duality of consciousness.

children.text: kiñcāsau kasya jīvasya ko jīvo yasya seti cet
children.translated_text: Moreover, whose individual self does this <s>avidyā</s> belong to? If you ask, 'What is the individual self to which it belongs?',
then indeed in this way there would be no solution, but mutual dependence.

children.text: na tu jīvād avidyā syāt na ca jīvas tayā vinā
children.translated_text: But ignorance cannot arise from the individual soul, nor can the soul exist without it.
Nor is there an analogy with seed and sprout, because the production of the soul is impossible.

children.text: brahmaṇaś cen na sarvajñaṃ kathaṃ tad baṃbhramīti tebhoḥ
children.translated_text: If it belongs to <s>Brahman</s>, then how is it not omniscient? How could that be deluded? This is your difficulty.
For you, its dependence on a cognition that identifies body and self and is produced by ignorance is not possible,
because scripture teaches that <s>Brahman's</s> state of omniscience is intrinsic to it.
Now if omniscience is false because it contains the appearance of difference,
why, for that very reason, is it not unfalsified, like difference of wording and the like?
Just as difference of wording, repetition, number, and the rest are differentiators of scriptural injunctions,

children.text: bhedāvabhāsagarbhāś ca yathārthāḥ tādṛśī na kim ||
children.translated_text: and, though containing the appearance of difference, are real, why should omniscience not be of the same kind?
If ignorance can exist even in the omniscient and eternally liberated one,

children.text: tejasīva tamas tasmān na nivarteta kenacit ||
children.translated_text: then, like darkness in light, it would not be removed by anything.
You say that the validity of statements about omniscience and the like is merely practical,
whereas the validity of statements of non-duality is ultimate;

children.text: niyāmakaṃ na paśyāmo nirbandhāt tāvakād ṛte ||
children.translated_text: but we see no principle of restriction here, apart from your own insistence.
Being the locus and being the counterpositive are mutually contradictory.

children.text: kathaṃ vaikarasaṃ brahma sad iti pratipadyate ||
children.translated_text: How, then, can the uniform <s>Brahman</s> be understood as real?
If it is the locus as the inward self and the counterpositive in the form of <s>Brahman</s>,
then this distinction of forms in what has been constructed, if it is born by the grace of ignorance,
well, that too depends on it; so mutual dependence follows again.
If, because ignorance is not a real entity, this is not a description of its nature,
where have you ever observed this as a fault in a real thing?
The fault called mutual dependence comes from presupposing what one has to prove.

children.text: na vastutvād avastutvād ity ato nedam uttaram ||
children.translated_text: Therefore 'because it is real' or 'because it is unreal' is no answer to this.

children.text: kiṃcāvidyā na cet vastu vyavaharyaṃ kathaṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: Moreover, if ignorance is not a real entity, how can it be an object of practical dealings?
And it is not accepted to be like practical dealings with an unreal sky-flower and the like.

children.text: nāpy avastviti coktau tu vastutvaṃ sidhyati dhruvam
children.translated_text: Nor, when one says 'it is not a real entity,' is real-entity-status certainly established.

children.text: niṣidhyate samastena nañā vastviti cen matam ||
children.translated_text: If the view is that the compound negation denies the whole, 'entity' included,
then the entity which is first denied by the compound negation

children.text: pratiprasūtaṃ vyastena punas tad iti vastutā ||
children.translated_text: is produced back again by the separated negation; thus it becomes an entity.

children.text: ato na vastu nāvastu na sadvācyaṃ na cāpyasat
children.translated_text: Therefore you must never intend to say that there is no distinction appearing here:

children.text: bhedo na kaścakāstīti vivakṣīr mā sma jātucit ||
children.translated_text: neither real entity nor non-entity, neither expressible as existent nor as nonexistent.
Moreover, this ignorance that you have resorted to as the mother that sustains the manifest world,

children.text: avidyā sā kim ekaiva naikā vā tad idaṃ vada
children.translated_text: tell us this: is it just one, or is it not one?

children.text: tadāśrayaśca saṃsārī tathaiko naika eva vā ||
children.translated_text: And is the transmigrating person who is its locus likewise one alone, or more than one?

children.text: sā ced ekā tatas saikā śukasya brahmavidyayā
children.translated_text: If it is one, then that single ignorance was already removed before

children.text: pūrvam eva nirasteti vyarthaste muktaye śramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: by <s>Śuka's</s> knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>; so your labor for liberation is useless.

children.text: syān mataṃ naiva te santi vāmadevaśukādayaḥ
children.translated_text: Perhaps you think: <s>Vāmadeva</s>, <s>Śuka</s>, and the others do not really exist,
so the objection that the beginningless ignorance was removed by their knowledge does not arise.
For the distinction between liberated and unliberated is imagined by my ignorance,
because it is seen, like the manifested distinctions seen in my own dream.

children.text: yat punar brahmavidyātas teṣāṃ muktir abhūd iti
children.translated_text: And as for the statement that their liberation occurred through knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>,
let it be explained away by the reasoning used for statements of liberation in a dream.
But with just such an inference, another person may prove that the world is imagined by his own ignorance.
How will you answer him?
Whatever reason you intend to show that it is caused by your ignorance,
that very reason would apply to his case too, just as in the proof of an omniscient being.
Thus, in your doctrine, which is obstructed by mutually contradictory statements,

children.text: mukham astīti yat kiṃcit pralapann iva lakṣyase ||
children.translated_text: you appear to be babbling whatever comes to your mouth.
And just as the liberation of those people is like a statement of liberation in a dream,

children.text: tathaiva bhavato 'pīti vyartho mokṣāya te śramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: so too is yours; hence your labor for liberation is useless.
Just as their liberation, though nonexistent before through knowledge of the self,
is spoken of as having occurred, so too your later liberation through knowledge of the self

children.text: abhāviny eva sā mithyā bhāvinīty apadiśyatām
children.translated_text: should be described as falsely future, even though it will not occur.
And you do have illustrative statements about things seen in dreams.

children.text: nanu nedam aniṣṭaṃ me yan muktir na bhaviṣyati
children.translated_text: You may say: This is not undesirable for me, that liberation will not occur,
since, because the self is eternally liberated, liberation is eternally accomplished.
This would be like bringing a spirit into a rite of appeasement:
by this very claim, the labor of acquiring knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is all the more useless.
But if, although it is eternally real, because it is obstructed by ignorance,
it is as though nonexistent, and its manifestation is accepted as the fruit of knowledge,

children.text: hastastham eva hemādi vismṛtaṃ mṛgyate yathā
children.translated_text: just as gold and the like already in one's hand may be searched for when forgotten,
and just as, when one recognizes that very thing in the hand, one becomes at rest,
so too, because the eternally accomplished nature of the self is not known,
the corresponding state of transmigrating persons is manifested by knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text: hanta keyam abhivyaktir yā vidyāphalam iṣyate
children.translated_text: Alas, what is this manifestation that is accepted as the fruit of knowledge,
for the self-luminous principle of consciousness, which stands in the place of its own nature?

children.text: saṃvit kiṃ saiva kiṃ vāhaṃ brahmāstītīti kīdṛśī
children.translated_text: Is it that very consciousness, or is it a cognition of the form 'I am <s>Brahman</s>'? What sort of thing is it?

children.text: yadi svarūpasaṃvit sā nityaiveti na tatphalam ||
children.translated_text: If it is consciousness as its own nature, then it is eternal, and so it is not the fruit of that knowledge.

children.text: atha brahmāham asmīti saṃvittir vyaktir iṣyate
children.translated_text: But if the manifestation is accepted as the cognition 'I am <s>Brahman</s>',

children.text: nanu te brahmavidyā sā saiva tasyāḥ phalaṃ katham ||
children.translated_text: surely for you that is knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>; how can that itself be its own fruit?

children.text: kiñca sā tat tvam asy ādivākyajanyā bhavan mate
children.translated_text: Moreover, in your view it is produced by sentences such as 'That thou art';
being produced, it is non-eternal, and so even the liberated person would have cause for fear.
Furthermore, those who understand practical affairs say that, when there is a full set of causes,

children.text: kāryaṃ na jāyate yena tam āhuḥ pratibandhakam ||
children.translated_text: that by which an effect does not arise is an obstruction.

children.text: iha kiṃ tad yad utpattum upakrāntaṃ svahetutaḥ
children.translated_text: Here, what is that thing which, having begun to arise from its own cause,
does not attain production because it is obstructed by ignorance?

children.text: na muktir nityasiddhatvāt na brahmāsmīti dhīr api
children.translated_text: Liberation is not so, because it is eternally established; nor is even the thought, "I am <s>Brahman</s>," liberation.
For the thought "I am <s>Brahman</s>" is not the abundant cause of consciousness.
Since that exists for a transmigrating person, how can it be obstructed?
Because, from the absence of a cause, it does not arise now;

children.text: na punaḥ pratibaddhatvād asthāne tena tadvacaḥ ||
children.translated_text: it is not, rather, because it is obstructed. Therefore that statement is out of place.

children.text: kiñcaiko jīva ity etad vastusthityā na yujyate
children.translated_text: Moreover, this claim that the individual self is one does not fit the state of reality,
for <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), its conjunction, individual-selfhood, and so on are false for you.
A merely apparent unity is contradicted by appearance,
since thousands of transmigrating beings appear to us.
And until the complete destruction of transmigration, practices produced by that plurality
are apprehended as uncontradicted and different from the occurrences in a dream.
Therefore even a unity based on reasoning is contradicted by reasoning.
Other embodied beings too, whose mutually opposed courses of thought are inferred from differences in activity,
cannot be denied, just like one's own self in each case.
Just as inferences are distinct from inferable things such as fire,

children.text: pratyakṣaṃ tekṣyante tathānyebhyo jīvebhyo na pṛthak katham ||
children.translated_text: and are directly observed by you, so how are they not distinct from other individual selves?
If another knowing subject is not inferred from a distinctive effort,
then all worldly and Vedic practice would be destroyed.
Nor is the cognition of the division between object of knowledge and knower due to a difference of limiting adjuncts,
because that would also apply in one's own body because of the difference of head, hands, and so on.
Just as, there, when sensation arises in the head, hand, foot, and so forth,
there is recollective connection because of unity, so it would be for you everywhere.
Because of the pain of death, the torments of hell, and even the distress of birth,
experiences of former births that passed long ago are not within the range of memory.
When pleasures, pains, and the like arise simultaneously,
there is a clear non-confusion of their substrates; how then can there be the error that they have a single object or owner?
Nor can this course of worldly life be made intelligible
by many individual selves each with its own objects of vision imagined by a private <s>avidyā</s>.
Ignorant of others' affairs, seeing only their own individual dreams,
how could they carry on that world-process, which depends on common connection and the like?
Moreover, self-luminosity, all-pervasiveness, oneness, and eternality,
which you accept, would contradict your non-duality of consciousness.

children.text: saṃvid eva na te dharmāḥ siddhāyām api saṃvidi
children.translated_text: They are not consciousness itself, nor are they its properties, since even when consciousness is established
dispute about them is observed, and because the things having those forms are different.

children.text: na ca te bhrāntisiddhās te yenādvaitāvirodhinaḥ
children.translated_text: Nor are those established by error, so that they would be consistent with non-duality;
for those qualities are established by Vedānta sentences that disclose reality.
But if bliss, self-luminosity, eternality, greatness, and the like
are accepted as the very nature of <s>Brahman</s>, then this too must be examined.

children.text: brahmeti yāvan nirdiṣṭaṃ tanmātraṃ kiṃ sukhādayaḥ
children.translated_text: Is what is denoted by the word "<s>Brahman</s>" only that much, namely happiness and the like?

children.text: atha vā tasya te yad vā ta eva brahmasaṃjñinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or are they attributes of it, or are those very things called <s>Brahman</s>?
On the first alternative, the mention of each of those words in the Veda and in ordinary speech would be purposeless,
and, by the reasoning stated earlier, there would also be difference, and <s>Brahman</s> would be the cause of the birth and so on of the world.

children.text: abhyupetyaiva hi brahma vivādās teṣu vādinām
children.translated_text: For the disputants engage in controversy about these only after accepting <s>Brahman</s> itself.

children.text: dvitīye saiva tair eva brahmaṇaḥ sadvitīyatā ||
children.translated_text: On the second alternative, by those very attributes, <s>Brahman</s> has a second.

children.text: tṛtīye brahma bhidyeta tanmātratvāt pade pade
children.translated_text: On the third, <s>Brahman</s> would be divided, since in each word it would be that alone,
or else the collection of them would be <s>Brahman</s>, like a forest that is a group of trees.

children.text: prakarṣaś ca prakāśaś ca bhinnāv evārkavartinau
children.translated_text: Excellence and luminosity, though present in the sun, are indeed distinct;

children.text: tena na kvāpi vākyārtho vibhāgo 'sti nidarśanam ||
children.translated_text: therefore there is nowhere an example where the meaning of a sentence is without division.
If, through the exclusion of inertness, pain, and the like,
words such as knowledge and bliss have their occurrence in one thing alone, then reality does not have a second.

children.text: apohāḥ kiṃ na santy eva santo vā nobhaye 'pi vā
children.translated_text: Are the exclusions themselves nonexistent, existent, or neither?
If they exist, reality would have a second; if they are of the nature of inertness and the like, it would be otherwise.
The statement that something is distinct from both existent and nonexistent has already been refuted before;

children.text: tathātve ca ghaṭādibhyo brahmāpi na viśiṣyate ||
children.translated_text: and if that were so, <s>Brahman</s> too would not be distinguished from pots and the like.
Moreover, if a meaning opposed to the inertness and so on to be excluded is not conveyed,
then that thing is not excluded at all, just as by words having the same meaning.
But when a counterpositive is seen, the cognition merely of another positive entity
is itself absence; so here too, by admitting real entities, you have reality with a second.
How is it ascertained that the differences of elements and elemental products
are distinct from both existent and nonexistent? Is it from perception and the rest, or from scripture?

children.text: pratyakṣādīni mānāni svaṃ svam arthaṃ yathāyatham
children.translated_text: The means of knowledge, perception and the like, each delimit
their own proper object as they arise; this much is witnessed by oneself.

children.text: yathāgrataḥ sthite nīle nīlimānyakathā na dhīḥ
children.translated_text: When blue is situated in front, cognition is not a cognition of some other blueness;

children.text: ekākārā na hi tayā sphaṭike dhavale matiḥ ||
children.translated_text: it has a single form, and by it there is not cognition of a white crystal.
The cognition of sweetness in milk is not at all like the cognition of bitterness in neem,
and all worldly and Vedic practices are fixed accordingly.

children.text: satyaṃ pratītir asaty asyā mūlaṃ nāstīti cen na tat
children.translated_text: If you say, "Granted, there is appearance, but there is no basis of this unreal appearance," that is not so.

children.text: sā ced asti tasyā mūlaṃ kalpyatāṃ kāryabhūtayā ||
children.translated_text: If the appearance exists, let its basis be postulated, since it is an effect.
And the sense organs, inferential marks, and so on are conceived as that basis, because it follows upon their presence.
Because simultaneity and sequence are impossible for the acts of delimitation and assignment,

children.text: aikyāyogācca bhedo na pratyakṣa iti yo bhramaḥ
children.translated_text: and because unity is impossible, the error that difference is not perceptible
arises from not grasping the distinction between difference and mutual absence.
The very own nature of things, shining forth through perception,
would be the cause of the expression of difference, in dependence on a counterpositive.
Just as cognition of that alone can establish the verbal usage "many" and "not one,"
or just as there are differences of shortness and length in a single object of six finger-breadths,
so, because it possesses many well-established modes and forms...
The being-thus of the perceptible manifold cannot be denied.

children.text: āgamaḥ kāryaniṣṭhatvād īdṛśe 'rthe na tu pramā
children.translated_text: Scripture, because it is directed toward what is to be done, is not a means of knowledge with respect to such a matter;
even if it had authority, it would not communicate this, because its subject matter is not fit for connection with the words.

children.text: nāsat pratīteḥ bādhācca na sadityapi yanna tat
children.translated_text: If it is not nonexistent because it is apprehended and because it is sublated, and if it is not existent either, then what is it?

children.text: pratīter eva sat kiṃ na bādhān nāsat kuto jagat
children.translated_text: Why is the world not existent precisely because it is apprehended, and how is it not nonexistent because it is sublated?
Therefore this <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) has been adopted by you only through <s>avidyā</s>.
Moreover, is the property of the manifold of difference, namely being false,

children.text: mithyā vā paramārtho vā nādyaḥ kalpo 'yam añjasā ||
children.translated_text: itself false or ultimately real? The first alternative is not straightforward.
If that falsity is false, the reality of the manifold is hard to deny;
and if it is ultimately real, then by that very fact your non-duality is destroyed.

children.text: sarvāṇy eva pramāṇāni svaṃ svam arthaṃ yathoditam
children.translated_text: All means of knowledge, just as they have been stated,
exclude their own respective objects from nonexistent things and from other things, and they appear to us.

children.text: tathā hīha ghaṭo 'stīti yeyaṃ dhīr upajāyate
children.translated_text: For example, the cognition that arises here, 'This pot exists,'

children.text: sā tadā tasya nābhāvaṃ paṭatvaṃ vānumanyate ||
children.translated_text: does not at that time admit either the nonexistence of that pot or its being a cloth.

children.text: nanv astīti yad uktaṃ kiṃ tanmātraṃ ghaṭa ity api
children.translated_text: If you say, 'When existence is stated, is only that much meant, or also potness?'
If it is only that much, non-duality of being follows; if it is something other,
then it is established as distinct from both existent and nonexistent.

children.text: yady evam asti brahmeti brahmaupaniṣadaṃ matam
children.translated_text: If so, the Upanishadic doctrine that '<s>Brahman</s> exists'
would, for you, entail that <s>Brahman</s>, like a pot, is indefinable as either existent or nonexistent.
By the Vedic descriptions such as bliss, truth, and knowledge,
you yourself have thus established that <s>Brahman</s> too is not of that nature.
And the statement that the manifold is distinct from existent and nonexistent falls away.

children.text: yad yathā kiṃcid ucyeta tatsarvasya tathā bhavet ||
children.translated_text: In whatever way anything at all is spoken of, everything would have to be so in that way.
Therefore the cognition 'it exists,' when arising with regard to pots and the like,
makes known the ultimate reality of the constitution of each particular thing.
The status of things is constituted by exclusions of what is of the same class and of a different class,

children.text: svaiḥ svair vyavasthitai rūpaiḥ padārthānāṃ tu yā sthitiḥ
children.translated_text: and by their own determinate forms;

children.text: sā sattā na svatantrānyā tatrādvaitakathā katham ||
children.translated_text: that is existence, not some other independent entity. How, then, can there be talk of non-duality there?
Nor can the apprehension of many kinds of forms be denied.

children.text: na vedyaṃ vittidharmaḥ syād iti yatprāgudīritam ||
children.translated_text: As for what was said before, that the object known cannot be a property of knowledge,

children.text: tenāpi sādhitaṃ kiṃcit saṃvido 'sti na vā tvayā
children.translated_text: has something thereby been established by you as belonging to consciousness, or not?

children.text: asti cet pakṣapātaḥ syān na cet te viphalaḥ śramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If it has, there would be partiality in your thesis; if not, your effort is fruitless.
Therefore cognitions, whose perceived differences are intrinsically clear,
do not become one with external things such as pots, which remain in their own states.
The rule of being apprehended together is certainly not due to each single cognition;

children.text: na ced asti sasāmānyaṃ sarvaṃ saṃvedanāspadam ||
children.translated_text: otherwise everything that falls within cognition would not possess a common character.
If, because of the rule of being apprehended together, the object were nothing other than consciousness,

children.text: yad etad aparādhīnasvaprakāśaṃ tad eva hi
children.translated_text: then only that which is self-luminous, independent of anything else,
is what the elders call by the word 'self-luminosity.'

children.text: yasminn abhāsamāne 'pi yo nāmārtho na bhāsate
children.translated_text: When some object does not appear if another is not appearing,

children.text: nāsāv arthāntaras tasmān mithyendur iva candrataḥ ||
children.translated_text: that object is not something different from it, just as a false moon is not different from the moon.
And when cognition is not appearing, there is no appearing of self or object;
therefore the manifold clearly proceeds as a transformation of consciousness.
Not so. This is a slighting of matters remembered or inferred in the face of the stronger perception.
Those objects, whose differences are protected by perception, do not conform to inference.

children.text: tathā hīdam ahaṃ vedmīty anyonyānātmanā sphuṭam
children.translated_text: For the threefold complex, 'I know this,' clearly shines forth directly
as mutually not identical, and this is witnessed by the self of everyone.
Inference does not operate in opposition to perception;

children.text: na hi vahner anuṣṇatvaṃ dravyatvād anumīyate ||
children.translated_text: for one does not infer that fire is not hot on the ground that it is a substance.

children.text: kiñca hetur viruddho 'yaṃ sahabhāvo dvayor yataḥ
children.translated_text: Moreover, this reason is contradictory, since there is coexistence of the two;

children.text: tavāpi na hi saṃvittiḥ svātmanā saha bhāsate ||
children.translated_text: for even according to you, consciousness does not appear together with itself as its own self.
In deep sleep and the like there appears a stream of pure clear consciousness,

children.text: svāpādau bhāsate naivam arthaḥ saṃvedanāt pṛthak
children.translated_text: free from disturbances such as blue and the like; an object apart from cognition does not appear in that way.

children.text: tena saṃvedanaṃ satyaṃ saṃvedyo 'rthas tv asann iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore cognition is real, but the object cognized is nonexistent.
This is the prattle of one who has not considered the contradiction in his own statement.
For, if that were so, the rule of apprehension would be lost.

children.text: yasmād ṛte yad ābhāti bhāti tasmād ṛte 'pi tat
children.translated_text: Whatever appears without something else also appears without that thing;

children.text: ghaṭād ṛte 'pi nirbhātaḥ paṭād iva ghaṭaḥ svayam ||
children.translated_text: just as a pot, though it appears apart from a cloth, itself shines forth apart from a pot.
